title: Literature May Help People Be More Forgiving — Study
paragraphs: Research has found that reading literature can help people understand others' thoughts and feelings. And in a recent study, researchers wanted to learn about the effect literature can have on readers' willingness to forgive.
Participants read a story about a woman named Mary. In the story, Mary had seen her puppy killed by a car as a child. She was so sad that she said she would never get another dog.
But at the age of 85, Mary finally got another puppy. Then a repairman left the door of Mary's home open, although Mary had told him to keep it closed. The puppy ran out.
If you were Mary, would you forgive the repairman?
It's a difficult question. But it helps us think about how Mary feels.
In the study, the researchers looked at whether readers would be more forgiving if they could read a character's private thoughts, instead of simply hearing them express their feelings out loud.
Different groups were given different versions of the story.
One version included this information: "The repairman said to Mary, 'I wish I didn't leave the door open.'"
Another version included the repairman's private thoughts: "The repairman thought to himself, 'I wish I didn't leave the door open.'"
Other parts of the story also varied. For example, in one version the man was presented as being careless, while in another, he was distracted by problems in his private life.
All the stories ended before the participants could find out if Mary forgave the man.
The researchers found that participants were more willing to forgive the repairman when they could read his private thoughts.
And more interestingly, people who were more willing to forgive the repairman were also found to be more willing to forgive someone they had a problem with in real life!
